historical_record.description: After a lawsuit over the city's title went to the U.S. Supreme Court, the city gained clear title to Alta Plaza, reserved as a public square by the Van Ness Ordinance of 1855.

Neighboring property owners paid for a survey and awarded a prize to R. Ulrich, probably the landscape designer Rudolph Ulrich, for a design for the park; the city graded and planted it and built walks, archways and bulkheads between 1891 and 1899.

The Parks Department, under John McLaren, had built four flights of terrace steps; in September the park commission approved a Beaux-Arts overlook at the crest by the sculptor Earl Cummings, which was never built.
Residents watched the city burn from Alta Plaza after the earthquake, and by evening homeless families filled the park.

A public lavatory was built, the first new work in the park after the earthquake, followed by tennis courts in 1910 and 1911 and two more courts and a basketball court in 1933; a playground replaced the basketball court and one tennis court in the 1950s.
The Recreation and Park Commission ratified a $181,700 contract with Tamal Construction Co. to rehabilitate Alta Plaza.

Answering the Supervisors' request to make Alta Plaza fit for playground use, the Board of Park Commissioners reported that plans were being drawn, with a citizens' committee, to enlarge its play area and add play apparatus.
